Tensor Module

The tensor module provides automatic differentiation capabilities with a NumPy backend and optional GPU acceleration.

Victor Core Tensor Module

Unified tensor and autograd engine with production-grade features.

This module consolidates best practices from multiple tensor implementations (tensor_autograd_engine.py, victorch, Qwen, OmegaTensor) into a single, robust, well-tested engine.

Key Features:

  • Complete backward pass with topological sort

  • Broadcasting support with gradient reduction

  • Standard operations (add, mul, matmul, sum, mean, reshape, transpose)

  • Activation functions (ReLU, Sigmoid, Tanh, Softmax)

  • Optimizers (SGD, Adam, RMSprop)

  • JVP (Jacobian-Vector Products) for forward-mode AD

  • Save/load functionality for model checkpoints

  • Zero external dependencies (NumPy only)

Example

>>> from victor_core.tensor import Tensor
>>> x = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> y = (x * 2).sum()
>>> y.backward()
>>> print(x.grad)  # [2., 2., 2.]
class victor_core.tensor.Tensor(data: ndarray | list | float | int, requires_grad: bool = False, dtype: dtype = <class 'numpy.float32'>)[source]

Bases: object

N-dimensional array with automatic differentiation support.

The Tensor class wraps NumPy arrays and tracks computational graphs for automatic gradient computation via backpropagation.

Parameters:

  • data – Input data (array-like or scalar)

  • requires_grad – Whether to track gradients for this tensor

  • dtype – NumPy dtype for the underlying data

data

Underlying NumPy array

grad

Accumulated gradients (None until backward is called)

requires_grad

Whether this tensor requires gradients

shape

Shape of the underlying data

Example

>>> x = Tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], requires_grad=True)
>>> y = (x * 2).sum()
>>> y.backward()
>>> print(x.grad)  # [[2., 2.], [2., 2.]]

backward(gradient: ndarray | float | None = None, retain_graph: bool = False) → None[source]

Compute gradients via backpropagation.

Performs reverse-mode automatic differentiation starting from this tensor and propagating gradients to all tensors with requires_grad=True in the computational graph.

Parameters:

  • gradient – Initial gradient (default: 1.0 for scalars, ones for arrays)

  • retain_graph – Keep computation graph for multiple backward passes

Example

>>> x = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> y = (x ** 2).sum()
>>> y.backward()
>>> print(x.grad)  # [2., 4., 6.]
jvp(v: Tensor) → Tensor[source]

Compute Jacobian-Vector Product (forward-mode AD) - PLACEHOLDER.

Note: This is a simplified placeholder implementation. Full JVP support requires dual numbers or similar forward-mode AD infrastructure, which is planned for Phase 2.

Parameters:

v – Vector to multiply with Jacobian

Returns:

Approximation of J @ v where J is the Jacobian

Warning

This implementation uses numerical differentiation and should not be used in production. It’s provided for API completeness only.

Example

>>> # For production use, implement proper dual numbers
>>> x = Tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> v = Tensor([1.0, 0.0])
>>> # result = x.jvp(v)  # Not recommended for actual use
victor_core.tensor.no_grad()[source]

Context manager to disable gradient tracking.

Example

>>> x = Tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> with no_grad():
...     y = x * 2
>>> print(y.requires_grad)  # False

Bases: Optimizer

Stochastic Gradient Descent optimizer.

Parameters:

  • parameters – List of tensors to optimize

  • lr – Learning rate

  • momentum – Momentum factor (default: 0)

Example

>>> params = [Tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)]
>>> optimizer = SGD(params, lr=0.01)
>>> # ... compute loss and call loss.backward()
>>> optimizer.step()
>>> optimizer.zero_grad()

victor_core.tensor.relu(x: Tensor) → Tensor[source]

Rectified Linear Unit activation.

ReLU(x) = max(0, x)

Parameters:

x – Input tensor

Returns:

Tensor with ReLU applied element-wise

Example

>>> x = Tensor([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> y = relu(x)
>>> print(y.data)  # [0., 0., 1.]

victor_core.tensor.softmax(x: Tensor, axis: int = -1) → Tensor[source]

Softmax activation function.

Converts logits to probabilities that sum to 1.

Parameters:

  • x – Input tensor (logits)

  • axis – Axis along which to apply softmax

Returns:

Tensor with softmax applied

Example

>>> x = Tensor([[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]], requires_grad=True)
>>> y = softmax(x)
>>> print(y.data.sum())  # 1.0
victor_core.tensor.mse_loss(y_pred: Tensor, y_true: Tensor) → Tensor[source]

Mean Squared Error loss.

MSE = mean((y_pred - y_true)^2)

Parameters:

  • y_pred – Predicted values

  • y_true – True values

Returns:

Scalar tensor with MSE loss

Example

>>> y_pred = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> y_true = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 2.0])
>>> loss = mse_loss(y_pred, y_true)
>>> print(loss.item())  # 0.333...
victor_core.tensor.binary_cross_entropy(y_pred: Tensor, y_true: Tensor, eps: float = 1e-07) → Tensor[source]

Binary Cross-Entropy loss.

BCE = -mean(y_true * log(y_pred) + (1 - y_true) * log(1 - y_pred))

Parameters:

  • y_pred – Predicted probabilities (0 to 1)

  • y_true – True labels (0 or 1)

  • eps – Small constant for numerical stability

Returns:

Scalar tensor with BCE loss

victor_core.tensor.cross_entropy(logits: Tensor, targets: Tensor) → Tensor[source]

Cross-Entropy loss (combines softmax and negative log-likelihood).

Parameters:

  • logits – Unnormalized scores (N, C) where C is number of classes

  • targets – Class indices (N,) with values in [0, C-1]

Returns:

Scalar tensor with cross-entropy loss

Note

This is a simplified version. Full implementation would handle class indices directly rather than one-hot encoding.

backward(gradient: ndarray | float | None = None, retain_graph: bool = False) → None[source]

Compute gradients via backpropagation.

Performs reverse-mode automatic differentiation starting from this tensor and propagating gradients to all tensors with requires_grad=True in the computational graph.

Parameters:

  • gradient – Initial gradient (default: 1.0 for scalars, ones for arrays)

  • retain_graph – Keep computation graph for multiple backward passes

Example

>>> x = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> y = (x ** 2).sum()
>>> y.backward()
>>> print(x.grad)  # [2., 4., 6.]

Compute Jacobian-Vector Product (forward-mode AD) - PLACEHOLDER.

Note: This is a simplified placeholder implementation. Full JVP support requires dual numbers or similar forward-mode AD infrastructure, which is planned for Phase 2.

v – Vector to multiply with Jacobian

Approximation of J @ v where J is the Jacobian

Warning

This implementation uses numerical differentiation and should not be used in production. It’s provided for API completeness only.

Softmax activation function.

Converts logits to probabilities that sum to 1.

>>> x = Tensor([[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]], requires_grad=True)

Loss Functions

victor_core.tensor.mse_loss(y_pred: Tensor, y_true: Tensor) → Tensor[source]

Mean Squared Error loss.

MSE = mean((y_pred - y_true)^2)

Parameters:

  • y_pred – Predicted values

  • y_true – True values

Returns:

Scalar tensor with MSE loss

Example

>>> y_pred = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> y_true = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 2.0])
>>> loss = mse_loss(y_pred, y_true)
>>> print(loss.item())  # 0.333...
victor_core.tensor.binary_cross_entropy(y_pred: Tensor, y_true: Tensor, eps: float = 1e-07) → Tensor[source]

Binary Cross-Entropy loss.

BCE = -mean(y_true * log(y_pred) + (1 - y_true) * log(1 - y_pred))

Parameters:

  • y_pred – Predicted probabilities (0 to 1)

  • y_true – True labels (0 or 1)

  • eps – Small constant for numerical stability

Returns:

Scalar tensor with BCE loss

victor_core.tensor.cross_entropy(logits: Tensor, targets: Tensor) → Tensor[source]

Cross-Entropy loss (combines softmax and negative log-likelihood).

Parameters:

  • logits – Unnormalized scores (N, C) where C is number of classes

  • targets – Class indices (N,) with values in [0, C-1]

Returns:

Scalar tensor with cross-entropy loss

Note

This is a simplified version. Full implementation would handle class indices directly rather than one-hot encoding.

>>> # ... compute loss and call loss.backward()

>>> optimizer.zero_grad()

Context manager to disable gradient tracking.

>>> with no_grad():
...     y = x * 2
>>> print(y.requires_grad)  # False
